NON-DISCLOSURE AGREEMENT
THIS NON-DISCLOSURE AGREEMENT, dated as of July 22, 2008, is by and between Varelin Investments Corporation (“Investor”) and Taylor Capital Group, Inc. (together with its wholly-owned subsidiary, Cole Taylor Bank, the “Company”).
WHEREAS, Investor has expressed an interest in discussing with the Company a possible financing transaction being considered by the Company (a “Transaction”);
WHEREAS, in connection with such discussions, the Company may disclose Evaluation Material (as defined below) to Investor; and
WHEREAS, the Company would not disclose the Evaluation Material to Investor, nor discuss with the Investor the possibility of a Transaction, unless Investor executed and delivered this Agreement to the Company, and the Company may be irreparably harmed if Investor or any of its Representatives (as defined below) were to take any of the actions prohibited under this Agreement.
NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual promises and covenants contained herein, and other good and valuable consideration, the receipt, sufficiency and adequacy of which is hereby acknowledged, intending to be legally bound, Investor and the Company hereby agree as follows:
1. Evaluation Material. For purposes of this Agreement, the term “Evaluation Material” shall mean any and all information provided to Investor by or on behalf of the Company in connection with the Transaction whether in writing, orally, visually, electronically or in machine readable form, through demonstration or in any other manner, and shall include, without limitation, any information regarding or relating to the Company’s operations, business opportunities, costs, finances, personnel, marketing and promotion plans, financial statements, financial information and business practices or policies, and any other business information of the Company or the terms or existence of this Agreement, the Company’s consideration of a possible Transaction or any discussions between the parties with respect thereto, transmitted by or on behalf of the Company to Investor in connection with the Transaction, whether prior to or after the execution and delivery of this Agreement and whether or not such information is marked “confidential”. The term “Evaluation Material” does not include, and the obligations hereunder do not apply to, information, knowledge or data which (i) was in Investor’s or its Representatives’ (as defined below) possession prior to disclosure by the Company, or (ii) was or becomes available to Investor or its Representatives on a non-confidential basis from a party other than the Company provided that such party is not known to Investor, after reasonable inquiry, to be under an obligation of confidentiality to the Company with respect to such information, or (iii) at the time of disclosure or thereafter is generally available to the public (other than as a result of disclosure by Investor or its Representatives in violation of this Agreement), or (iv) Investor can demonstrate has been independently developed by it or on its behalf without reliance on the Evaluation Material. All Evaluation Material transmitted by or on behalf of the Company shall remain the sole property of the Company.
2. Use of Evaluation Material. The Evaluation Material will be used by Investor solely in connection with its evaluation of a possible Transaction, and not for any other purpose whatsoever. The Evaluation Material will be kept confidential by Investor in accordance with the terms and conditions of this Agreement and will not be disclosed to any person, except that Investor may disclose the Evaluation Material or portions thereof to those of its employees, officers, directors, partners, members, affiliates, accountants, attorneys, agents, consultants and advisors (these persons being collectively called “Representatives”) who (a) need to know such information in order for Investor to be
able to evaluate a possible Transaction and (b) have been directed by Investor to treat the Evaluation Material in accordance with the terms of this Agreement. For the avoidance of doubt, the term “Representatives” as applied to Investor shall not include any potential principal, co-investor or source of equity financing that is not a party to this Agreement. Investor shall be responsible for any breach of this Agreement by any of its Representatives. Neither Investor nor any of its Representatives shall, directly or indirectly, (x) market or use (other than as permitted by the Agreement) any Evaluation Material, (y) reproduce or otherwise copy any Evaluation Material except in connection with the Transaction, or (z) disclose, sell, license, offer to sell or license or otherwise transfer or make available any Evaluation Material to any person other than as otherwise permitted by this Agreement. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, Investor will use all reasonable efforts to protect the confidentiality of Evaluation Material, including, without limitation, efforts commensurate with those it employs for the protection of its own confidential and proprietary information. The term “person” as used in this Agreement will be interpreted broadly to include, without limitation, any agency, corporation, individual, partnership, limited liability company, joint venture or other entity.
3. Exceptions. If Investor or its Representatives receive a subpoena or other validly issued administrative or judicial process requesting Evaluation Material, or if Investor or its Representatives are requested or required to disclose any Evaluation Material under law, governmental order, judicial order, regulatory or statutory requirement, discovery request, oral questions, interrogatories, requests for information or documents, subpoena, civil investigative demand or similar process, Investor shall notify the Company reasonably promptly following Investor or its Representatives first becoming aware of such requested disclosure, so that the Company may seek a protective order or other appropriate remedy or, in the Company’s sole discretion, waive compliance with the terms of this Agreement. Furthermore, if the Company seeks such a protective order or other appropriate remedy in connection with a third-party request or requirement to disclose the Evaluation Material, Investor and its Representatives will not oppose such efforts. In the event that no such protective order or other remedy is obtained, or that the Company waives compliance with the terms of this Agreement, and Investor or its Representatives are advised by legal counsel that they are legally compelled to make such disclosures, Investor or its Representatives, as the case may be, (i) may without liability hereunder furnish only that portion of the Evaluation Material or other information regarding a possible Transaction that Investor or its Representatives are advised by legal counsel is legally required, (ii) will give the Company notice of the disclosures to be made to the extent legally permissible and (iii) will, if applicable, request that confidential treatment be accorded the Evaluation Material or other information regarding a possible Transaction so disclosed to the extent legally permissible; it being understood and agreed that there can be no such assurance that the tribunal or governmental or similar authority will grant any such request.
4. No Warranty. ALL EVALUATION MATERIAL IS PROVIDED “AS IS,” AND THE COMPANY HEREBY DISCLAIMS ANY AND ALL WARRANTIES, EXPRESS, IMPLIED OR OTHERWISE, INCLUDING BUT NOT LIMITED TO ANY WARRANTIES REGARDING ITS ACCURACY, COMPLETENESS, PERFORMANCE OR NON-INFRINGEMENT OF THIRD PARTY RIGHTS OR ITS MERCHANTABILITY OR FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE.
5. No Legal Obligation, Representation, or Warranty. The parties agree that, unless and until a binding agreement is entered into between the Company and Investor with respect to the Transaction, neither the Company nor Investor will be under any legal obligation of any kind whatsoever with respect to the Transaction by virtue of this or any other written or oral expression, except with respect to the matters specifically agreed to herein. Nothing contained in any discussions between Investor and the Company or in any Evaluation Material shall be deemed to constitute a representation or warranty. Except for the matters set forth in this Agreement or in any such binding agreement, neither party shall be entitled to rely on any statement, promise, agreement, or understanding, whether oral or written, or any custom, usage of trade, course of dealing, or conduct.
6. Return of Evaluation Material. At any time upon the written request of the Company, Investor will, at its own expense,
(i) reasonably promptly redeliver to the Company or, at the at Investor’s option, destroy all copies (including permanently erasing or deleting any electronic copies) of the Evaluation Material in the possession or control of Investor or any of its Representatives and
(ii) reasonably promptly destroy all analyses, notes, data, compilations, summaries, forecasts, studies or other documents and materials prepared by Investor or any of its Representatives in connection with their evaluation and review of a possible Transaction that contain, reflect or are based upon or generated from, in whole or in part, any of the Evaluation Material. Upon the Company’s written request, Investor will confirm any such destruction to the Company in writing. Notwithstanding the return or destruction of Evaluation Material, Investor will continue to be bound by its obligations of confidentiality hereunder respecting Evaluation Material, including without limitation, with respect to oral Evaluation Material and their obligation not to use any Evaluation Material for any purpose other than as specifically permitted in this Agreement.
7. Non-Solicitation. For a period of eighteen months from the date of this Agreement, Investor will not, without the Company’s prior written consent, directly or indirectly, solicit for purposes of employment, offer to hire or offer to enter into any contract with any executive officer of the Company with whom Investor has contact, or of whom Investor otherwise becomes aware, during its discussions with the Company or its evaluation of a possible Transaction; provided, however, that this paragraph shall not prohibit Investor from engagement in any general advertising or general solicitation not targeted to the Company’s employees; and provided, further, that Investor shall not be prohibited from soliciting or hiring any such employee whose employment has been terminated by the Company or its affiliates.
8. Standstill. For a period of eighteen months from the date of this Agreement, and except in connection with the Transaction, Investor will not, directly or indirectly, and Investor will cause any person controlled by Investor not to, without the prior written consent of the Board of Directors of the Company, (i) in any manner acquire, agree to acquire or make any proposal to acquire, directly or indirectly, any securities or property of the Company or any of its affiliates, (ii) propose to enter into, directly or indirectly, any merger, consolidation, recapitalization, business combination, partnership, joint venture or other similar transaction involving the Company or any of its affiliates, (iii) make, or in any way participate in any “solicitation” of “proxies” (as such terms are used in the proxy rules of the Securities and Exchange Commission) to vote, or seek to advise or influence any person with respect to the voting of any voting securities of the Company or any of its affiliates, (iv) form, join or in any way participate in a “group” (within the meaning of Section 13(d)(3) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended) with respect to any voting securities of the Company or any of its affiliates, (v) otherwise act, alone or in concert with others, to seek to control or influence the management, Board of Directors or policies of the Company, (vi) disclose any intention, plan or arrangement inconsistent with the foregoing or (vii) advise, assist or encourage any other person in connection with any of the foregoing. Investor also agrees during such period not to (x) request the Company, directly or indirectly, to amend or waive any provision of this paragraph (including this sentence), (y) take any action that would reasonably be expected to require the Company or any of its affiliates to make a public announcement regarding this Agreement or the possibility of a Transaction, or (z) communicate with the Company’s stockholders (other than communications with any of the officers of the Company, and any other employees of the Company designated by such officers, in the manner contemplated by this Agreement) regarding the subject matter of this Agreement.
9. Acknowledgement. Investor acknowledges that it is aware, and that it will advise its Representatives who receive the Evaluation Material, that the United States securities laws prohibit any person who has received from an issuer material, non-public information from purchasing or selling securities of such issuer (and options, warrants and rights relating thereto) or from communicating such information to any other person under circumstances in which it is reasonably foreseeable that such person is likely to purchase or sell such securities.
10. Public Disclosure. Each of the Company and Investor acknowledge and agree that it will not, and it will cause its respective employees, representatives, affiliates and agents not to, publicly disclose, confirm or acknowledge the existence, or terms and conditions, of this Agreement, or the fact that the Company may be considering a possible Transaction with Investor, other than in a press release approved by each party hereto or as otherwise specifically agreed in writing by the parties hereto, except to the extent the Company believes in good faith, after consultation with counsel, it is required by any law, rule or listing requirement to make such disclosure, provided that the Company shall not identify the Investor or any of its affiliates by name without the Investor’s consent.
11. No License. Investor acknowledges and agrees that nothing contained in this Agreement will be construed as granting any rights, by license or otherwise, to Investor or any of its Representatives to any Evaluation Material, or to any copyrights, trademarks, service marks, patent rights, trade secrets, or other proprietary rights of the Company.
12. Third-Party Contacts. Neither Investor nor any of its Representatives shall knowingly contact any employee (other than the officers of the Company and other employees designated by such officers in the manner contemplated by this Agreement), supplier or customer of the Company regarding the Transaction or the Company’s prospects, without the Company’s prior written consent.
13. No Commitment. Each of the Company and Investor understands and agrees that no contract or agreement or binding obligation providing for or with respect to any Transaction shall be created or deemed to exist unless and until a definitive agreement has been executed and delivered with respect thereto, and that, unless and until a definitive agreement between the parties has been executed and delivered, no party has any legal obligation of any kind whatsoever to enter into or pursue a Transaction by virtue of this Agreement or any other written or oral expression, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement.
14. Equitable Remedies. Investor hereby agrees that a failure to comply with any provision of this Agreement would cause the Company irreparable harm and that monetary damages would be an inadequate remedy for an actual or threatened breach of this Agreement by Investor or any of its Representatives because of the difficulty of ascertaining the amount of damage that will be suffered by the Company in the event that this Agreement is breached. state:
The fictional suite Merovan is organized around a refrain that returns with a different harmonic accompaniment each time. Its opening melody begins on the tonic, pauses on the second degree, and resolves through a repeated third. The accompaniment alternates between a sustained chord and a sequence of detached notes. Neither accompaniment replaces the melodic refrain; both provide contrasting rhythmic settings for it. The final cadence retains the opening melody's last interval while changing the chord that supports it. This gives the suite a recognizable connection between its introduction and its conclusion without making their harmonies identical.

In Merovan's opening episode, the pulse continues through the rests in the melody. A recurring pattern of two sounded beats and one silent beat creates an expectation that the next phrase sometimes postpones. The melody answers that expectation with a note held across the accompaniment's next attack. On a later return, the accompaniment keeps the same pattern while the melody articulates every beat. The contrast comes from the placement of attacks and rests, rather than a change in the pulse. Both versions conclude with the same rhythmic cadence, giving their different patterns a shared point of arrival.

A subsequent episode uses a melody whose accented notes imply a different grouping from the accompaniment. The accompaniment continues its regular alternation of consonant chords, while the melody places emphasis on notes that occur between those chord changes. The resulting tension is rhythmic even when the harmonies are stable. When both parts finally articulate the cadence together, their agreement is audible without any change in instrumentation. A later recurrence reverses which part maintains the regular pattern. The melody then provides continuity while the accompaniment introduces the displaced accents, preserving the episode's rhythmic identity through a different distribution of roles.

The refrain's harmonic variants have distinct functions within the fictional suite. A tonic accompaniment gives the melody a sense of repose; a dominant accompaniment makes the same melodic notes seem directed toward a resolution. A variant built on the relative minor gives emphasis to a different member of the same pitch collection. The refrain remains recognizable because its sequence of intervals and its rhythm are retained. Its emotional coloring changes through the supporting harmony. Merovan therefore presents recognizability and variation together: the recurring musical idea is neither a literal repetition of an entire episode nor an entirely new melodic subject.

A subsequent episode uses a melody whose accented notes imply a different grouping from the accompaniment. The accompaniment continues its regular alternation of consonant chords, while the melody places emphasis on notes that occur between those chord changes. The resulting tension is rhythmic even when the harmonies are stable. When both parts finally articulate the cadence together, their agreement is audible without any change in instrumentation. A later recurrence reverses which part maintains the regular pattern. The melody then provides continuity while the accompaniment introduces the displaced accents, preserving the episode's rhythmic identity through a different distribution of roles.

The refrain's harmonic variants have distinct functions within the fictional suite. A tonic accompaniment gives the melody a sense of repose; a dominant accompaniment makes the same melodic notes seem directed toward a resolution. A variant built on the relative minor gives emphasis to a different member of the same pitch collection. The refrain remains recognizable because its sequence of intervals and its rhythm are retained. Its emotional coloring changes through the supporting harmony. Merovan therefore presents recognizability and variation together: the recurring musical idea is neither a literal repetition of an entire episode nor an entirely new melodic subject.

The final cadence retains the opening melody's last interval while changing the chord that supports it. This gives the suite a recognizable connection between its introduction and its conclusion without making their harmonies identical.

In Merovan's opening episode, the pulse continues through the rests in the melody. A recurring pattern of two sounded beats and one silent beat creates an expectation that the next phrase sometimes postpones. The melody answers that expectation with a note held across the accompaniment's next attack. On a later return, the accompaniment keeps the same pattern while the melody articulates every beat. The contrast comes from the placement of attacks and rests, rather than a change in the pulse. Both versions conclude with the same rhythmic cadence, giving their different patterns a shared point of arrival.

A subsequent episode uses a melody whose accented notes imply a different grouping from the accompaniment. The accompaniment continues its regular alternation of consonant chords, while the melody places emphasis on notes that occur between those chord changes. The resulting tension is rhythmic even when the harmonies are stable. When both parts finally articulate the cadence together, their agreement is audible without any change in instrumentation. A later recurrence reverses which part maintains the regular pattern. The melody then provides continuity while the accompaniment introduces the displaced accents, preserving the episode's rhythmic identity through a different distribution of roles.

The refrain's harmonic variants have distinct functions within the fictional suite. A tonic accompaniment gives the melody a sense of repose; a dominant accompaniment makes the same melodic notes seem directed toward a resolution. A variant built on the relative minor gives emphasis to a different member of the same pitch collection. The refrain remains recognizable because its sequence of intervals and its rhythm are retained. Its emotional coloring changes through the supporting harmony. Merovan therefore presents recognizability and variation together: the recurring musical idea is neither a literal repetition of an entire episode nor an entirely new melodic subject.

Merovan's concluding episode recalls the detached accompaniment from the opening, but combines it with the refrain's sustained rhythmic variant. The cadence is prepared by an alternation of dominant and tonic sonorities whose rhythm echoes the first episode. A rest interrupts the expected final attack, after which the melody completes its familiar interval. The accompaniment then sustains the tonic while the refrain ceases. This ending preserves several previously heard relationships among rhythm, melody, and harmony without replaying an earlier episode in full. Its continuity depends on the recurrence of particular musical features rather than on identical orchestration at every return.

Merovan's harmonic introduction establishes a tonic without immediately giving it a definitive cadence. The opening sonority is followed by a chord that shares two of its tones, allowing the accompaniment to change while the melodic refrain remains recognizable. A subsequent dominant prepares a resolution that the melody postpones through a rest. The tonic is eventually confirmed by the rhythm of the cadence as much as by the chord itself. This distinction matters to the suite's design: harmonic arrival and rhythmic completion can coincide, but their separation provides a recurring source of expectation throughout the episodes.

The second presentation of the refrain retains its interval sequence while altering the duration of its notes. The first note receives the duration previously assigned to the second, and the third is articulated twice before the phrase continues. These changes preserve the order of the pitches but alter the perception of emphasis. A note that previously sounded like a passing connection becomes a point of repose. The accompaniment responds with its familiar cadence, making the rhythmic reinterpretation audible against a harmonic process that has already been established in the introduction.

A contrasting melody in the suite uses repeated pitches rather than the refrain's characteristic intervals. Its identity comes from an alternating pattern of articulation and silence. At first, every repeated pitch is accompanied by a chord change. On its return, several repetitions share a single harmony, and the melody seems more insistent despite retaining the same pitches. The change does not require an additional melodic subject. It demonstrates how harmonic rhythm can transform the character of a phrase whose pitch content remains stable, complementing the refrain's earlier variations of duration.

The suite's transitional music makes deliberate use of incomplete cadences. A dominant sonority sometimes resolves to a chord that sounds provisional rather than final, allowing a new episode to begin without a decisive interruption. Elsewhere, a rhythmic cadence occurs while the harmony continues to imply another resolution. These transitions are not interchangeable. One maintains harmonic expectation through a change of texture, while the other maintains continuity through an apparently completed phrase. Their different functions help distinguish episodes that share the refrain from episodes built around the repeated-pitch melody.

In a later harmonic variant, the refrain is accompanied by a progression that avoids its expected dominant until the final phrase. Earlier phrases end on a consonant sonority that offers repose without confirming the tonic. The resulting continuity depends on the listener recognizing the refrain's cadential rhythm even when its harmonic support differs. When the dominant finally appears, its significance comes from the contrast with those previous endings. The suite does not introduce a new refrain at that moment; it changes the harmonic consequence of a familiar melodic and rhythmic gesture.

An episode centered on imitation presents the repeated-pitch melody in alternating entries. Each entry retains the same articulation pattern, but the entries begin at different points in the accompaniment's harmonic cycle. One therefore sounds conclusive where another sounds preparatory. The imitation is organized by the relationship between entry and cadence, rather than by a continuous succession of identical phrases. A rest after the final entry allows the accompaniment to complete its progression alone. That unaccompanied harmonic completion recalls the introduction's separation of melodic expectation from harmonic arrival.

The refrain's pauses are treated as compositional material in their own right. A pause can interrupt the expected continuation of the melody while the accompaniment sustains a consonance, producing anticipation without harmonic tension. Another pause occurs over a dominant sonority, so melodic interruption and harmonic expectation reinforce one another. The distinction is preserved even when the pauses have equal duration. Merovan's variations consequently depend on the context of silence as well as the presence of sound. A repeated rhythmic pattern need not carry an identical sense of continuation on each return.

One passage alternates the refrain with brief responses derived from its final interval. The responses omit the refrain's opening notes and use a different rhythm, yet their connection remains audible through that interval. Initially, the accompaniment treats each response as the beginning of a new phrase. Later, it harmonizes the response as a cadence, giving the same melodic fragment a different formal role. The alternation ends when the refrain and response share a single cadential progression. Their earlier distinction is retained in rhythm even as their harmonic functions converge.

Merovan introduces a modal variant without replacing the refrain's central rhythmic gesture. A changed scale degree alters the harmony's color, while the refrain's pattern of attacks and rests remains familiar. The accompaniment emphasizes the changed degree through a recurring consonance rather than an isolated accent. When the earlier pitch collection returns, the rhythmic continuity makes the harmonic contrast apparent. The modal episode therefore develops material already present in the suite. It does not depend on treating a change of pitch collection as the introduction of an entirely different musical identity.

The repeated-pitch melody receives a contrasting treatment in which each articulation has a different duration. Some notes are detached, others are sustained, and rests divide the repetitions into unequal groups. The accompaniment nevertheless follows a regular harmonic rhythm. Its consistency gives the varying durations a common temporal reference. During the reprise, the melody resumes equal durations while the accompaniment changes chords irregularly. The relationship between continuity and variation is exchanged between the two parts, recalling the suite's earlier exchange of rhythmic roles without reproducing that episode's exact material.

A cadential fragment from the opening serves as the basis of a separate transition. It is repeated with a different harmony each time, but the repetitions do not all imply completion. A consonant support makes one occurrence sound settled, while a dominant support makes the next sound provisional. The fragment's rhythm remains identical, so the change in function can be attributed to its harmonic context within the fictional composition. The transition concludes when the fragment is omitted and the accompaniment completes the expected progression without its melodic cadence.

The suite uses consonance in several distinct ways. A consonant chord can confirm an arrival, sustain continuity during a melodic rest, or prepare a later change by establishing a stable pitch collection. These roles are differentiated by rhythm and recurrence. The same chord does not announce a conclusion every time it appears. In one episode, a succession of consonant harmonies accompanies a melody that repeatedly postpones its final note. The resulting phrase remains active until the melodic rhythm and harmonic progression finally articulate a cadence together.

A passage of harmonic suspension retains a tone from one sonority while its accompaniment changes. The retained tone initially creates tension against the new harmony, then resolves as the accompaniment sustains. A later suspension uses the same rhythm but delays the melodic resolution until after another chord change. The two versions therefore differ in their coordination of harmonic and melodic events. Neither introduces a new refrain. Both elaborate a relationship already suggested by the introduction, where melodic completion and harmonic arrival were deliberately separated before being reunited at a cadence.

The suite's recurring rhythmic figure sometimes appears without its characteristic melody. The accompaniment adopts the pattern of attacks and rests, while a contrasting subject proceeds with sustained notes. This transfer allows the rhythmic figure to connect otherwise distinct episodes. On the refrain's next appearance, its rhythm is recognizable before the familiar interval sequence is completed. The connection is musical rather than verbal: no narrative event is attached to the figure. Its significance arises from the recurrence of duration, articulation, and silence across different harmonic and melodic settings.

Merovan's treatment of sequence depends on variation rather than mechanical continuation. A melodic fragment is restated at a different pitch level, but its accompaniment changes the expected harmonic consequence of the restatement. Another sequence preserves the accompaniment's progression while altering the fragment's final interval. These processes allow repetition to generate contrast without introducing an unrelated subject. The sequence ends with a phrase whose rhythm recalls its first statement, making the termination audible even though its harmony differs from the harmony that began the passage.

An episode in compound meter groups its pulse differently from the preceding music while retaining the refrain's characteristic accent. The melody's familiar emphasis is redistributed within the new grouping, and its pauses acquire a different relationship to the accompaniment. The transition into this episode uses a shared rhythmic gesture rather than an abrupt cessation. On returning to the earlier meter, the accompaniment retains a trace of the compound grouping through its pattern of articulation. The meter changes, but a recognizable rhythmic relationship persists across the transition.

The suite distinguishes between a refrain's complete return and the recurrence of a fragment. A complete return preserves the interval sequence and cadential rhythm, even when the harmony changes. A fragment may retain only an opening interval, a repeated pitch, or the rhythm of a pause. These fragments prepare later returns without supplying an entire refrain each time. Their distribution gives the composition continuity between its more clearly defined episodes. The final return is consequently recognizable through several features that have been heard separately as well as together.

A contrasting harmonic episode centers on the relative minor while retaining the refrain's concluding rhythm. The accompaniment gives emphasis to a pitch that had previously acted as a passing tone. In this context, that pitch sounds stable, and the refrain's familiar cadence acquires a different coloring. The return to the tonic is prepared by a progression that includes both pitch collections. This preparation preserves continuity without making the two harmonic contexts indistinguishable. The contrast depends on the function assigned to shared pitches, rather than on the mere presence of different notes.

The repeated-pitch melody is later presented as a dialogue between alternating musical parts. One part articulates the initial repetitions, and the other completes the rhythmic pattern after a rest. Their exchange is recognizable because the combined rhythm matches the earlier melody, although neither part states it alone. A reprise changes the distribution of those articulations without altering their combined order. The melody's identity therefore survives a redistribution of responsibility within the texture. Its final cadence reunites the parts in a simultaneous articulation that had previously been withheld.

Merovan's transitions sometimes use harmonic commonality to connect contrasting rhythms. A sustained consonance can support the refrain's cadential figure and then continue beneath the repeated-pitch melody. The change of subject is audible through articulation rather than through a new harmony. In another transition, the rhythm remains constant while the accompaniment changes its tonal emphasis. These alternatives show that continuity can be maintained through different musical features. The suite avoids relying on a single transitional device, even when its episodes derive from the same recurring materials.

An episode of rhythmic diminution presents the refrain with reduced note durations while preserving its sequence of intervals. The accompaniment retains its earlier pace, allowing several melodic gestures to occur within one harmonic progression. The resulting activity contrasts with an earlier sustained version of the refrain. At the cadence, the melody resumes its familiar durations, and the two parts articulate the conclusion together. The episode changes the distribution of melodic events without requiring a new pitch collection or a different harmonic destination for the recurring subject.

A complementary episode uses augmentation, sustaining the refrain's notes through several changes of accompaniment. Individual melodic tones consequently encounter different harmonic contexts before the melody proceeds. A tone that begins as a consonance may become a suspension and later resolve without being articulated again. This treatment emphasizes continuity within the melody while allowing the harmony to provide variation. The cadence is prepared by reducing the accompaniment's activity, so that the refrain's concluding interval can be heard as a completion rather than merely another retained tone.

The suite gives the repeated-pitch melody a harmonic variant based on an ostinato. The accompaniment repeats a rhythmic pattern whose final sonority changes on successive returns. The melody's repeated notes remain stable, but their harmonic interpretation varies as the ostinato changes. Eventually, the final sonority stops changing and confirms the tonic. The episode's sense of arrival therefore results from the cessation of harmonic variation within a continuing rhythm. The melody does not need a new cadence at that point, because the accompaniment supplies the formal completion.

An episode built around offbeat articulation begins with the accompaniment withholding the expected attack. The melody enters during that absence and sustains into the accompaniment's next articulation. The resulting syncopation is maintained through several harmonic changes. Later, the same melodic rhythm is paired with an accompaniment that articulates the expected beats. Its character changes even though the melody remains literal. Merovan uses this contrast to distinguish rhythmic displacement created by one part from the coordination of both parts, making their eventual agreement a recognizable formal event.

The refrain's opening interval is sometimes harmonized as a preparation and sometimes as an arrival. In one context, the interval begins a progression that requires further melodic motion. In another, it follows a cadence and confirms a tonic that is already established. The interval's acoustical identity does not determine its formal role by itself. Rhythm, preceding harmony, and subsequent continuation all contribute to that role. The suite's recurring use of the interval therefore creates connections without requiring every occurrence to carry the same harmonic or expressive function.

A passage of contrasting articulation places detached notes in the melody against sustained harmonies. The rhythm is unchanged from an earlier episode in which both parts used sustained articulation, yet the new presentation gives the melodic attacks a different prominence. The reprise exchanges those articulations between the parts. The accompaniment becomes detached while the melody sustains its notes. Their cadential rhythm remains common to both versions. This treatment develops the suite's interest in distributing continuity and interruption between musical roles, rather than assigning either quality permanently to one part.

Merovan includes a transition in which the cadence's expected final chord is delayed through a repeated rest. Each repetition preserves the duration of the rest but changes the harmony that precedes it. The melody responds by varying its final interval, preventing the transition from becoming an identical cycle. The expected tonic eventually arrives without an additional melodic attack. Its effect depends on the preceding succession of preparations and interruptions. The final sonority completes a harmonic process whose melodic counterpart has already been suggested in several different forms.

One episode places the refrain in a pentatonic setting. Several pitches that had supported earlier harmonies are absent from this episode's collection, but the refrain's characteristic rhythm is retained. Its interval sequence is adapted at the point where an omitted pitch would otherwise occur. The resulting version remains connected to the refrain through rhythm and contour, while its harmonic vocabulary is distinct. A subsequent transition restores the omitted pitches gradually through accompaniment changes. The familiar tonal context returns as a musical process rather than as an unexplained replacement.

The suite's treatment of melodic ornament separates an underlying interval sequence from its elaboration. A recurring melodic tone may be preceded by a neighboring tone, delayed by a suspension, or repeated after a brief rest. The accompaniment preserves the harmonic progression associated with the refrain, making these elaborations audible as variations of familiar material. On the final return, most ornaments are omitted. The simplified presentation recalls the introduction while carrying the listener's memory of the intervening variants. Its continuity depends on recognizable relationships, not on literal identity of every articulation.

A later episode gives the accompaniment a melodic role derived from the refrain's concluding interval. The primary melody retains its repeated-pitch pattern, while the accompaniment introduces the interval at the ends of its phrases. Their interaction connects subjects that had previously appeared separately. The resulting texture is not a simultaneous statement of two complete refrains. It combines a fragment with a distinct rhythmic subject, allowing each to retain its identity. At the cadence, the accompaniment's fragment is omitted, leaving the repeated-pitch melody to articulate the conclusion alone.

Merovan contrasts harmonic predictability with rhythmic ambiguity in an episode whose progression repeats without alteration. Each recurrence begins at a different point in the melody's accent pattern. The same chord can therefore coincide with an accent, an unaccented continuation, or a rest. The progression remains recognizable, but its relationship to the phrase changes. The episode concludes when harmonic recurrence and rhythmic grouping coincide at a cadence. That coincidence resolves an organizational tension without requiring a change in the pitch material used by either part.

Another episode reverses this arrangement by retaining a regular rhythmic grouping while varying the harmony of successive phrases. The melody repeats its accent pattern and cadence, but its accompaniment alternates between tonic, relative-minor, and dominant-centered settings. Each setting gives a different consequence to the same rhythmic completion. The episode's final phrase returns to the opening tonic context, making the harmonic itinerary audible through recurrence. Its organization depends on the order of the harmonic settings, while the regular rhythm supplies continuity across their changes.

A transition based on overlapping phrase endings allows one melodic gesture to begin before another has completed its cadence. The accompaniment supports both gestures through a harmony shared by their pitch collections. Their overlap does not erase their different rhythms. One gesture retains the refrain's sustained cadence, while the other introduces the repeated-pitch subject's detached articulation. The transition is completed when the earlier gesture ceases and the new subject continues alone. This procedure connects episodes without requiring a pause or an identical restatement of either complete subject.

The suite's modal episode returns with a change in harmonic rhythm. Its initial presentation assigned one harmony to each melodic phrase; its recurrence changes harmony within the phrases. The melody remains literal, but some of its tones acquire different functions as the accompaniment proceeds. A tone that previously confirmed a chord can become a preparation for the next one. This recurrence develops the earlier episode through altered coordination, rather than through a new melodic invention. The cadence retains its original rhythm, allowing the changed harmonic process to remain perceptible.

A passage of rhythmic contraction reduces the pauses between successive fragments of the refrain. The fragments themselves retain their note durations, so the increased continuity comes from the treatment of silence. The accompaniment follows the same harmonic progression at first, then delays its final dominant to accommodate the altered phrasing. When the expected pause returns at the cadence, its effect is established by contrast with the preceding contractions. The passage develops the refrain's temporal organization without changing the order of its characteristic melodic intervals.

The repeated-pitch subject acquires a contrasting variant in which its articulations are grouped around a sustained tone. That tone is not accented on every recurrence, and its changing relationship to the repeated notes gives the phrase a different rhythm. The accompaniment initially sustains a tonic, then introduces a dominant beneath the same melodic grouping. The familiar notes consequently participate in a different harmonic preparation. The cadence resolves both the repeated-note pattern and the sustained tone, connecting the variant to the suite's recurring concern with simultaneous and separated completions.

Merovan uses a deceptive cadence to redirect one episode into a further variation of the refrain. The melody articulates the rhythm associated with completion, but the accompaniment supplies a harmony that implies continuation. The refrain then begins without a rest, retaining the pitch that the cadence had emphasized. This connection makes the new variation sound like a consequence of the interrupted ending. On the episode's eventual reprise, the same cadential rhythm receives a tonic resolution instead. The contrast gives the two occurrences different formal purposes despite their shared melodic gesture.

A contrasting transition omits the melody entirely while retaining the accompaniment's rhythmic identity. Its harmonic progression recalls the refrain, but no complete melodic subject is presented. The return of the melody is prepared through the recurrence of its characteristic pause in the accompaniment. When the refrain enters, its first note coincides with a harmony that has already been established. The effect differs from an entrance that simultaneously introduces a new tonal context. Merovan thus distinguishes preparation through accompaniment from preparation through a fragment of the melody itself.

The suite's final harmonic variants increasingly combine processes introduced in separate episodes. A sustained refrain can be accompanied by the ostinato's rhythm, while the ostinato's changing final sonority is replaced by a stable tonic. The repeated-pitch subject can retain its detached articulation while adopting the modal episode's pitch collection. These combinations are specific rather than indiscriminate. Each preserves a recognizable rhythmic or interval relationship from its source material. The concluding cadence brings selected relationships together without attempting to repeat every previous variation in a single musical statement.

A retrospective passage recalls the introduction's delayed resolution but changes which part supplies the final articulation. In the introduction, the accompaniment completed its progression after the melody paused. In this recurrence, the accompaniment sustains while the melody resolves its final interval. The relationship between interruption and continuation remains recognizable even though the roles are exchanged. The passage prepares the coda by presenting completion as a shared process rather than the property of one recurring part. Its significance depends on comparison with earlier musical events within the fictional suite.

The coda begins with the refrain's rhythm detached from its complete interval sequence. Only the opening pitch and cadential interval remain, separated by the characteristic pause. The accompaniment supports them with the tonic progression heard in the introduction. This reduction emphasizes the features that have connected the suite's variations without introducing a new subject. A subsequent phrase restores the omitted intervals, but the accompaniment ceases its detached pattern. The refrain's final complete statement is therefore recognizable through restored melodic detail and altered articulation at the same time.

Merovan's final rest is prepared by the gradual cessation of recurring rhythmic figures. The ostinato's pattern is omitted first, followed by the repeated-pitch subject's detached articulations. The refrain remains until its concluding interval resolves against the tonic. A sustained consonance then continues without another melodic attack. This ending does not replay the introduction, although it recalls the same tonic and characteristic interval. Its completion depends on the accumulated relationships among the variations and on the audible withdrawal of the rhythmic processes that had sustained the suite's continuity.

The harmonic character of Merovan also depends on how the members of a chord are distributed among its musical parts. A triad can support the refrain with its root emphasized, or allow its third to give prominence to another melodic tone. The harmonic function need not change with that redistribution. In the refrain's modal recurrence, however, a different emphasis clarifies the altered scale degree and makes the modal contrast audible. The suite consequently uses the distribution of chord tones both to preserve familiar harmony and to distinguish a particular variant from its earlier presentation.

A seventh added to the accompaniment's dominant creates a preparation that differs from a simple triadic dominant. In Merovan, the added tone is sometimes sustained into the tonic before resolving, allowing the harmonic cadence to precede the completion of an individual musical part. On another occurrence, that tone resolves before the tonic arrives. These alternatives give the cadence different internal rhythms even when the progression itself is unchanged. The treatment extends the introduction's separation of harmonic arrival from melodic completion through the behavior of a particular chord member.

Chromatic neighboring tones appear in a variation of the repeated-pitch subject. The repeated pitch remains the point of return, while a semitone inflection interrupts some of its articulations. The accompaniment initially sustains a harmony that treats the inflection as an embellishment. Later, a chord change makes that same inflected tone part of the harmony. Its role therefore depends on the coordination of melody and accompaniment. The variation does not abandon the repeated-pitch subject; it develops the contrast between a stable recurrence and a tone whose harmonic significance can change during the phrase.

One harmonic episode sustains a tonic pitch through a succession of contrasting sonorities. Some harmonies include the sustained pitch as a consonance, while others create tension against it. The refrain continues with its characteristic rhythm, giving the episode continuity in both melody and accompaniment. When the sustained pitch finally ceases, the next harmony is heard without that persistent reference. The change marks a transition even though the refrain itself continues. The suite uses the duration of a harmonic reference as a formal resource, distinct from either the recurrence of a complete chord or the repetition of a melodic phrase.

The counterpoint in Merovan distinguishes sustained consonant intervals from dissonances created by melodic motion. A dissonant interval may occur as a passing consequence of one part's continuation, or be emphasized through a suspension whose resolution is delayed. The accompaniment's harmonic rhythm determines how those events participate in the phrase. A passing dissonance can become conspicuous when a chord change coincides with it, while a suspension may remain intelligible across a sustained harmony. These differences allow the suite to vary tension without replacing its recurring melodic subjects or their cadential rhythms.

A contrapuntal recurrence exchanges the melodic functions assigned to two musical parts. The refrain's concluding interval, previously heard as the primary gesture, becomes a response to the repeated-pitch subject. The response retains its rhythm but begins at another stage of the harmonic progression. As a result, the exchange alters formal emphasis as well as melodic responsibility. The recurrence is connected to the earlier episode through the recognizable behavior of both subjects, yet it does not reproduce their previous coordination. Their agreement at the cadence completes the exchange rather than cancelling its difference.

Canonic imitation in a separate passage uses an entry delayed by the duration of the refrain's characteristic pause. The second entry therefore begins at a moment associated with silence in the first. Their combination preserves each entry's rhythm while changing the continuity of the overall texture. The accompaniment supports the resulting alternation with a regular harmonic progression. A later cadence ends the imitation by allowing one entry to complete without another beginning. The ending is audible as the cessation of a recurring relationship between entries, rather than the introduction of a different melodic subject.

A retrograde treatment of a brief rhythmic fragment occurs during a transition, but the refrain itself is not presented in reverse. The fragment's durations are reordered so that its characteristic pause precedes rather than follows the detached articulations. Its new rhythm responds to the accompaniment's expected cadence in a different way. The transition then restores the familiar duration order before the refrain returns. This limited transformation gives the episode a distinct rhythmic identity while preserving the recognizability of the complete refrain when it is subsequently stated in its established form.

The suite includes an intervallic inversion of the refrain's opening gesture. Its rhythm remains familiar, while the melodic intervals change their direction. The accompaniment gives the transformed gesture a harmonic setting that distinguishes it from the complete refrain. On the next return, the established interval sequence and the transformed gesture alternate as separate responses. Their relationship is apparent through rhythm and interval size, but their formal roles differ. The transformed gesture prepares a continuation where the established gesture had previously announced an arrival, giving the relationship a specific purpose within the episode.

An anacrusis changes the way one refrain variant begins. Notes preceding the first regular accent give the opening interval a sense of preparation rather than an immediate statement. The accompaniment maintains its established harmonic rhythm, so the alteration is heard as a change in melodic phrasing. During the reprise, the preparatory notes are retained but the accompaniment delays its first chord. The resulting coordination differs from both the initial refrain and its first anacrustic variant. Their common interval sequence continues to provide recognition despite these different relationships between preparation and accent.

Merovan uses a hemiola near the cadence of its compound-meter episode. Accents temporarily suggest a grouping that contrasts with the continuing pulse. The melody's durations remain compatible with both groupings, allowing the accompaniment's articulation to determine which grouping is most apparent at a particular moment. The cadence restores their agreement without a change of tempo. This rhythmic event differs from the earlier transition between meters, because the underlying pulse continues while its accented organization is reinterpreted. Its function is to intensify a cadence that is already harmonically prepared.

An episode with alternating metric groupings combines phrases of unequal duration. The accompaniment repeats a harmonic pattern whose changes do not always coincide with the beginnings of those phrases. The melody's cadential rhythm remains recognizable, but successive cadences arrive at different stages of the accompaniment's pattern. The episode ends when a final phrase allows those processes to coincide. Its organization is distinct from the regular meter heard in the introduction. Continuity comes from familiar melodic gestures and harmonic relationships rather than a uniform pattern of phrase beginnings throughout the suite.

The conservatory occupies a shallow courtyard between a brick residence and a former workshop. Its glazed roof rests on slender iron ribs, while the lower walls retain the texture of old lime plaster. The entrance faces a sheltered gravel court. Through the door, a broad stone path leads toward a recessed bench beneath the far gable. Planting beds lie beside the path, separated from it by low terracotta edging. The interior feels enclosed without feeling cramped: the roof exposes the sky, and the neighboring walls give the planting a sheltered boundary.

The entrance door has a heavy timber frame and a narrow pane of textured glass. Its handle is polished where hands naturally rest, but the surrounding metal retains a subdued finish. A deep threshold separates the gravel court from the interior paving. Beside the door, a shallow alcove accommodates a brush, a folded cloth, and a rack of garden footwear. The alcove is part of the wall rather than a freestanding cupboard, leaving the entrance passage clear. A slight projection above the doorway shelters the outer face of the timber from direct rain.

The main path consists of broad limestone slabs with softened edges. Their surface has a faint granular texture, and the joints contain a compact lime mortar. Near the planting beds, the paving has a narrow drainage channel with a removable grating. The channel follows the wall instead of crossing the entrance. The bed edging rises only slightly above the path, making the soil visible from the bench. Along the workshop wall, the slabs meet an older strip of brick paving whose uneven surface gives that side of the room a more domestic character.

The roof glazing is held in timber glazing bars laid over the iron frame. At the ridge, small ventilation panels sit beneath projecting caps. The caps shelter the opening edges while leaving a passage for air. The roof has a steeper pitch above the central path and a lower profile where it meets the neighboring walls. Narrow gutters follow the eaves. Their supporting brackets are visible from inside, where they form a quiet rhythm against the uninterrupted glass. The metalwork has a muted finish rather than a reflective coating.

The planting beside the residence wall is dominated by broad leaves and arching stems. Ferns occupy the shaded ground beneath taller foliage, and moss softens the exposed soil around the bed edges. The leaves differ in texture: some are smooth and leathery, others finely divided, with delicate veins visible against the roof light. None of the beds is raised on a stand. The plants emerge directly from a continuous soil surface, which gives the room the feeling of a small sheltered garden rather than a collection of movable containers.

The workshop side holds a potting recess behind a timber screen. The screen is made of narrow vertical slats with open spaces between them, allowing the recess to remain visually connected to the room. A stone shelf spans the back wall. Beneath it, shallow compartments accommodate empty pots, folded sacks, and a coiled length of hose. The shelf has a rounded front edge and a slightly recessed surface near the wall. Its worn finish differs from the smoother paving of the central path, making the working corner distinct without an additional doorway.

The bench beneath the far gable is built into a masonry recess. Its seat is timber, supported by brackets fixed beneath the front edge. The recess has a curved plaster ceiling that catches reflected light from the roof. A plain woven cushion covers the middle of the seat, and a narrow ledge runs along the wall behind it. The bench faces the entrance through the foliage. From that position, the path remains visible, while the planting beds soften the view of the surrounding brickwork. The recess provides a resting place without requiring movable furniture in the central passage.

A shallow basin is set against the wall near the potting recess. Its stone rim projects over a tiled backing, and the faucet has a simple cross handle. The tiles have an irregular glaze that appears smoother near their edges. A drain opening lies beneath a small removable strainer. The basin is supported by a masonry pedestal, leaving no exposed cabinet below it. The adjacent wall has a broad plaster patch around the plumbing connection. The patch remains visible as part of the room's accumulated repairs rather than being disguised by a decorative panel.

The residence wall contains an interior window overlooking the conservatory. Its deep reveal has a gently sloping sill, with plaster carried continuously around the corners. The frame is narrower than the entrance frame, and its glass is clear rather than textured. Inside the reveal, a slim curtain is gathered against the masonry. The window gives the neighboring room a view of the foliage and roof supports. Around it, the wall surface retains the small undulations of hand-applied plaster, contrasting with the more regular joints of the brickwork near the courtyard entrance.

The conservatory has no suspended ceiling beneath the glazing. Cables for the wall lamps follow the iron supports in close-fitting channels, and the fittings remain below the gutter line. Each lamp has a shallow ceramic shade that directs light toward the path rather than into the roof. The shades are plain, with a slightly uneven rim that reveals their handmade character. Their mounting plates are small enough to leave the surrounding plaster visible. The electrical fittings belong to the wall surfaces and do not interrupt the continuous view through the roof.

Near the bench, a climbing plant follows a wire support fixed away from the plaster. The wire is held by short projecting brackets, leaving room between the stems and the wall. The plant's woody base emerges from the bed beneath the recess, while its finer growth spreads toward the gable. The support is deliberately slender. It remains visible through gaps in the foliage without competing with the heavier roof frame. At the base, the soil is covered by a loose layer of leaf fragments whose dry texture contrasts with the glossy leaves above.

The workshop doorway is sealed by an interior panel rather than by another glazed door. The panel sits within the old opening, leaving the original lintel and worn jambs exposed. Its timber surface is flush with the adjoining screen, but a shallow shadow marks the former threshold. The outline of the opening gives the wall a recognizable history without turning it into a display. Above the lintel, a small area of rough masonry remains uncovered. It provides a tactile contrast to the lime plaster that extends toward the roof junction.

The bed near the entrance includes herbs with narrow leaves and compact branching stems. Their containers are sunk into the surrounding soil, so their rims are mostly hidden. A strip of crushed stone lies between this bed and the drainage channel. The stone has a varied surface, with rounded fragments mixed among sharper pieces. The planting is dense enough to soften the boundary between soil and paving, but the edging remains visible. The herbs give the entrance corner a distinct scent and a finer leaf texture than the larger foliage farther inside.

The roof junction above the residence wall has a stepped flashing tucked into the masonry. The exposed metal follows the roof slope without covering the entire brick face. Small mortar fillets close the remaining gaps around the ribs. From inside, the flashing appears as a narrow band at the upper edge of the plaster. The junction is practical rather than decorative, and its visible construction fits the room's simple materials. The neighboring chimney remains outside the glazing, rising beyond the roof without an opening into the conservatory itself.

A low timber chest sits within the potting recess, beneath the stone shelf. Its lid is flat, with a recessed grip instead of a projecting handle. The chest has broad corner joints and a slightly raised base that keeps its underside away from the paving. Its surface carries the shallow dents of ordinary use. The compartments beside it contain pots of differing shapes, some with thick rims and others with gently flared sides. Their arrangement leaves the shelf above unobstructed. The recess remains compact and functional rather than resembling a separate utility room.

The far gable includes a small fixed pane beneath the ridge. Its glass is set within a deep timber frame, with the lower edge aligned to the curve of the bench recess. Through it, the neighboring roof and a narrow strip of sky are visible. The pane admits light without providing a view into another interior. Around the frame, the plaster has a smoother finish than the lower walls, reflecting the brighter light of the gable. The contrast helps distinguish the upper enclosure from the more sheltered planting area below.

The garden footwear rack near the entrance is made of bent metal rods fixed to a shallow wall plate. The rods curve upward at their ends, keeping the footwear away from the plaster. Beneath the rack lies a removable tray with a ribbed surface. The tray fits within the alcove and does not project onto the limestone path. A folded cloth rests on the ledge above it. These small fittings make use of the depth of the entrance wall, while their modest scale leaves the doorway and its timber frame visually dominant.

The paving near the basin has a slightly rougher finish than the slabs beside the bench. A narrow border of brick follows the basin pedestal and meets the workshop wall at a softened corner. The border is flush with the surrounding stone, with no raised curb. Along the wall, a shallow recess accommodates the hose connection beneath a simple protective cover. The cover is shaped to fit the plaster opening rather than to resemble a freestanding box. Its subdued appearance is consistent with the other practical fittings of the room.

The courtyard outside the entrance has a sheltered corner beneath the residence eaves. A stone seat rests against the wall there, facing the conservatory door. The gravel surface meets a broad paving slab at the threshold, and a low planting strip follows the opposite boundary. The courtyard wall is lower than the workshop roof, allowing the conservatory gable to remain visible from the approach. The exterior materials echo those inside: brick, timber, stone, and muted metal. The glazing is the brightest surface, with reflections that partly obscure the foliage behind it.

The room's character comes from the close relationship between its practical construction and its planting. Roof supports, drainage, storage, and resting places remain visible rather than being hidden behind decorative finishes. The foliage gives the enclosure softness, while the stone path and masonry recess provide a stable outline. There is no large central object competing with the plants or the sky above them. The entrance, working corner, and bench each have their own material character, yet they belong to the same modest courtyard room, held together by continuous paving and the shelter of the glazed roof.
